subject: AME Chicago Chapter — Fall Manufacturing Summit speaker invite
snippet: Dear Evelyn, My name is Denise Whitcomb and I coordinate programming for the AME Chicago Chapter's Fall Manufacturing Summit, which this year runs September 15-16 at the Renaissanc
body_text:
Dear Evelyn,

My name is Denise Whitcomb and I coordinate programming for the AME Chicago Chapter's Fall Manufacturing Summit, which this year runs September 15-16 at the Renaissance Schaumburg Convention Center. I'm reaching out because your name came up twice independently — once from a member who attended your session at our spring roundtable, and once from Marta Klein at Ridgefield, who mentioned the process work your firm did there when I asked around for speaker recommendations focused on mid-market manufacturers specifically, which is a gap in our usual programming.

I'd like to invite you to join a panel on Day 1 (September 15th, 2:00-3:15pm) titled "Lean Without the Fortune 500 Budget: Operational Excellence for Mid-Market Manufacturers." The format is a moderated panel with three practitioners — so far confirmed are a plant director from a tier-two auto supplier and an operations VP from a mid-sized food processor — followed by 20 minutes of audience Q&A. We typically get 80-120 attendees in that room, mostly plant managers, ops directors, and a handful of owner-operators from companies in the 50-500 employee range, which I understand overlaps closely with your client base.

Logistics: we cover a modest honorarium ($750) plus one night at the Renaissance if you'd like to stay over rather than commute, and of course a full conference pass so you can attend other sessions and network. We'd need a short bio (100 words or so) and headshot by August 1st for the printed program, and I'd like to get 20 minutes on the phone with you and the other two panelists sometime in early September to align on what ground each of you will cover so we're not duplicating material on stage.

A little more on the audience, since it might affect how you'd want to pitch the material: about a third of the room last year were owner-operators rather than hired ops leadership, so questions tend to skew practical and skeptical of anything that sounds like a big consulting engagement — "what can I actually do Monday morning" is the recurring theme in our post-session surveys. Panelists who lean into concrete, low-cost first steps rather than a full transformation pitch tend to score much better with this crowd than the ones who sound like they're selling a retainer. I mention that only because I think it plays to your strengths given what Marta described, not because I think you need the advice.

I know this is a bit of a leap of faith without having seen you present, but based on what I've heard I think you'd be a strong addition to this particular panel. Would you be willing to join us? Happy to hop on a call if you have questions about format, audience, or anything else before deciding.

Best,
Denise Whitcomb
Programs Committee, AME Chicago Chapter
programs@ame.org

meta.action_summary: Evelyn needs to confirm the AME panel invitation and send a bio and headshot by August 1st.

snippet: Evelyn — pulled the raw logs before responding to Bob so we're not guessing. Short answer: yes, the retrofit week (June 2–6) is in the sample, but I don't think it moves the number
body_text:
Evelyn — pulled the raw logs before responding to Bob so we're not guessing.

Short answer: yes, the retrofit week (June 2–6) is in the sample, but I don't think it moves the number as much as he thinks. Here's the breakdown.

We logged 214 changeovers across Lines 2, 4, and 6 over the three-week window. The retrofit week contributed 31 of those changeovers on Line 4 only (Lines 2 and 6 ran normal crews all three weeks). If I strip out just those 31 events, Line 4's average changeover time drops from 51.2 minutes to 46.8 minutes — still 34% over benchmark, not the near-benchmark number Bob is hoping for. The fleet-wide average across all three lines only moves from 38.4 to 37.1 minutes, which is 21% over the benchmark of 30.7 instead of 22% over 31.5. That's not a material change to the finding or the recommendation.

That said, I think we should still run the excluded-week version as a supplementary table. Two reasons: first, it protects us if this becomes a credibility fight rather than a data fight — we want to be able to say we checked and the story doesn't change. Second, and more importantly, it actually strengthens our case: if a training week barely moves the number, it tells Bob's team the problem is structural, not a one-off staffing issue, which is exactly the argument we need to make for the tooling-cart recommendation to land.

I can have the revised table with both versions side by side by Monday. My worry is less about the math and more about how we frame it — if we come back too defensively it reads like we're backpedaling, and if we come back too flatly it reads like we're dismissing his floor supervisors, who aren't wrong that the retrofit week was unusual. I'd suggest we lead with 'good catch, we checked, here's what we found' rather than a straight defense of the original number.

One more data point while I'm in the logs: I also broke the sample out by line supervisor rather than just by line, since I wanted to rule out a single crew driving the whole variance. It's fairly even — no one supervisor's shifts are wildly out of line with the others, which is actually useful for us. It means we can tell Bob's team this isn't about any one crew underperforming, it's a tooling and setup problem that shows up consistently regardless of who's running the line. That's a much easier story for their floor supervisors to accept than 'your people are slow,' and it dovetails cleanly with the tooling-cart recommendation — the fix is process, not personnel.

I also went back and checked whether the retrofit week affected Lines 2 and 6 indirectly, since some of Line 4's pulled crew members occasionally cover other lines when short-staffed. No material overlap — the two crew members pulled for training weren't scheduled on 2 or 6 that week, so those lines' numbers are clean regardless of how we treat Line 4.

Want me to draft the response to Bob, or do you want to take the first pass since you have the relationship?

Kyle Brenner
Senior Consultant, Thorne & Cadwell Advisory

subject: AME Insights: Q3 Lean Manufacturing Trends
snippet: AME INSIGHTS — Q3 2026 Welcome back to AME Insights, your quarterly digest on lean manufacturing and operational excellence trends across North America. RESHORING MOMENTUM CONTINUE
body_text:
AME INSIGHTS — Q3 2026

Welcome back to AME Insights, your quarterly digest on lean manufacturing and operational excellence trends across North America.

RESHORING MOMENTUM CONTINUES
Our latest member survey of 340 manufacturers shows 38% have reshored at least one product line in the past 18 months, up from 24% last year. The primary driver remains supply chain risk rather than pure cost — respondents cited lead-time volatility and single-source dependency as the top two concerns, ahead of labor cost differentials. For consultants advising clients on facility strategy, this suggests total-cost-of-ownership models that weight resilience alongside unit cost are increasingly what wins board approval.

WORKFORCE: THE SKILLS GAP ISN'T CLOSING
Despite record investment in automation, 61% of member plants report unfilled skilled-trades positions, with CNC machinists and industrial electricians the hardest to fill. Several members have had success with in-house apprenticeship programs partnered with community colleges — Ridgefield Manufacturing's program, profiled in this issue, cut time-to-productivity for new hires from 9 months to 5.

DIGITAL THREAD ADOPTION
Adoption of digital thread / MES integration remains uneven. Plants under 100 employees report only 22% adoption versus 58% for plants over 500 employees, largely due to upfront implementation cost and lack of internal IT resources. This is a real opportunity area for outside advisors who can de-risk the business case and phase implementation around cash flow constraints rather than a big-bang rollout.

UPCOMING EVENTS
- AME 2026 Chicago Summit, October 6-9, McCormick Place
- Regional Lean Roundtable (Midwest chapter), September 12, Rockford IL
- Webinar: "Building the Business Case for Digital Thread," August 28

MEMBER SPOTLIGHT
This quarter we profile a mid-market automotive supplier that cut changeover time 34% through a SMED initiative led by an outside consulting team — a useful case study to reference with clients weighing whether outside help is worth the fee. The engagement ran 14 weeks, involved three plant floor workshops, and the client credits the outside facilitator with getting operators to buy in where two prior internal attempts had stalled. We also spotlight a packaging manufacturer that used a rolling six-week diagnostic before committing to a larger transformation program, a structure several members have told us they're now requesting explicitly from their advisors rather than accepting a full-scope proposal up front.

CHAPTER NEWS
The Midwest chapter welcomes two new board members this quarter, both plant operations leaders from member companies. The chapter's fall calendar includes plant tours, a benchmarking roundtable on labor cost trends, and a joint session with the local ASCM chapter on integrating lean and supply chain planning — a combination several consulting members have asked us to cover more often given how frequently the two disciplines show up together in client engagements.

CERTIFICATION UPDATES
The Lean Bronze Certification exam window opens again in September, and early registration discounts are available for members through August 31. AME is also piloting a new credential aimed specifically at external advisors and consultants, recognizing that a growing share of our membership works client-side rather than as in-house practitioners. If that's a track you'd find useful, reply to this email — we're collecting interest before finalizing the curriculum.

RESEARCH NOTE
A recurring theme in this quarter's member interviews: leadership teams are asking for faster proof of ROI before greenlighting the next phase of any improvement program, a shift from the multi-year transformation roadmaps common a few years ago. Advisors who can show measurable wins within a single quarter are reporting stronger renewal rates on follow-on work.

As always, thank you for being an AME member. Questions or story ideas for future issues can be sent to insights@ame.org.

AME Insights Editorial Team
Association for Manufacturing Excellence

subject: Re: Halberd — hours vs. budget on the fixed-fee SOW
snippet: Adding Fiona for visibility since she's been running point on the process-mapping workstream and has the cleanest view of where the hours are going. Root cause, as best I can tell:
body_text:
Adding Fiona for visibility since she's been running point on the process-mapping workstream and has the cleanest view of where the hours are going.

Root cause, as best I can tell: it's scope, not pace. Here's the breakdown by workstream against original SOW estimate:

Process mapping: budgeted 60 hrs, actual 71 hrs so far. This is close to plan — slightly over because Halberd's floor layout changed since we scoped in April and we had to re-walk two areas.

Floor walks and time studies: budgeted 50 hrs, actual 74 hrs. This is the big one. The original SOW scoped three production lines (bottling, casing, palletizing). When we showed up week 1, Lucia told us corporate had just approved standing up two more lines (a second bottling line and a new co-pack line) and asked us to fold them in — she assumed that was a small ask. It wasn't; it's roughly 40% more floor to cover.

Financial model build: budgeted 60 hrs, actual 38 hrs. Under budget, on track, no issue.

Stakeholder interviews: budgeted 50 hrs, actual 27 hrs. Also fine, ahead of schedule.

One thing worth flagging separately: even setting the two extra lines aside, our original per-line estimate for floor walks was probably a touch light to begin with — we budgeted 50 hrs across three lines assuming roughly a day and a half per line including time-study passes, and in practice the bottling line alone has taken closer to two full days because of how much manual changeover work is happening there versus what we saw in the walkthrough during scoping. It's not the main driver of the overage, but I don't want it to get lost — I'd bake in a bit more cushion on floor-walk hours the next time we scope a line-level engagement, even before you get into unscoped additions.

So the total picture: 220 hrs budgeted, 140 burned, but if you back out the two extra lines nobody scoped for, we'd be sitting closer to 175 hrs used against 220 — basically on plan. The overage is almost entirely the two additional lines Lucia added in week 1 without a change order.

My read: we need a scope conversation with Lucia this week, not a schedule conversation with our own team. The team isn't moving slow, we're covering 40% more ground than the SOW priced for. I'd rather flag it now while there's still time to either scope-cut or get a change order than eat it silently and have this conversation in week 6 when it's too late to do anything but write it off.

Happy to pull together a one-pager Evelyn could take to Lucia if that's useful.

Kyle Brenner
Senior Consultant, Thorne & Cadwell Advisory

body_text:
Lucia,

Thank you for raising this directly — you're right to ask, and I owe you a full explanation rather than a vague reassurance. I went back through Kyle's and Fiona's time logs this morning with our office manager before writing this, so let me walk you through exactly where the hours went.

The original scope, as you say, was 120 hours built around mapping the three core production processes we discussed in kickoff. Two things happened that weren't in the original plan. First, in week two your plant manager asked us to extend the mapping to the packaging line as well, on the logic that the bottleneck we were finding upstream might actually originate there. That's a reasonable ask and I don't fault him for it, but it's genuinely additional scope — we estimate it added about 26 hours. Second, we had two full-day site walkthroughs that ran long because your second-shift supervisors weren't available during the originally scheduled windows, so Kyle and Fiona had to come back on separate days rather than combining the visits, which cost us roughly another 14 hours in travel and setup overhead we hadn't planned for.

As of yesterday we're at 142 of the 120 budgeted hours, with an estimated 18-24 hours of work remaining to close out the deliverable properly, which puts the likely final total somewhere around 160-166 hours against a 120-hour budget.

Here's what I'd propose. The packaging-line extension was a genuine scope change that your team requested, so I think it's fair for that piece (the ~26 hours) to be billed as a modest change order — call it $9,800 — rather than absorbed by us. The scheduling-related overrun (the ~14 hours plus whatever portion of the remaining work is attributable to it) I think is fair for us to eat, since better planning on our side could have avoided some of it even given the supervisor availability issue. Concretely: I'd like to invoice the original $68,000 fixed fee in full, add a single change order of $9,800 for the packaging line extension, and absorb the rest ourselves rather than billing it. That keeps the fixed-fee spirit of our agreement intact while being honest about the one piece that was a genuine scope addition on your side.

I'm glad to walk through the time logs on a call if that's useful, or just take this by email if it's clear enough as written. Either way, I want you to feel like the fixed fee actually meant something here, not just a number we abandon the moment it gets inconvenient.

Evelyn

Evelyn — flagging something before Friday's call with Lucia so you're not blindsided.

We're over on the Halberd fixed-fee engagement. Budgeted hours were 240 across the three of us (me, Fiona, and the 15 hours we allocated for Anil's data pull) for the full six-week scope. As of yesterday we're at 268 logged hours with just over three weeks left on the calendar, which puts us on pace to land somewhere between 310 and 330 by close-out — call it 70-90 hours over budget at our blended rate.

Two things are driving it. First, scope creep: Lucia's ops team asked us in week two to add a full SKU-level cut of the inventory turns analysis (the same one that's now separately on fire — see Ana's forward from a few days back), which wasn't in the original SOW and probably accounts for 30-35 of the extra hours by itself. Second, and this is more on us, Fiona underestimated how messy their WMS export was going to be — she's spent almost two full days just reconciling duplicate SKU codes before she could even start the real analysis.

I see three ways to handle it and wanted your read before I'm in front of Lucia:

1. We eat it. Blended rate puts the overage at roughly $16,800-$21,600 in unbilled time. Cleanest relationship-wise, worst for our margin on what's already a thin fixed-fee deal.

2. We raise a change order specifically for the SKU-level cut, since that genuinely wasn't in scope. I'd guess we could reasonably bill $8,000-$10,000 of it that way without it feeling like a shakedown, since they did ask for it.

3. We trim the remaining scope — specifically, drop the secondary warehouse-layout recommendations section, which was always the "nice to have" piece — to bring total hours back closer to budget without billing anything extra.

My instinct is some combination of 2 and 3, but I don't want to propose anything to Lucia without knowing where you land, especially given how the Meridian and Stratus stuff is stacking up on the firm's plate right now. Can you give me a steer before Friday at 3? I'd rather walk in with a plan than wing it.

Kyle

IN THIS ISSUE

FEATURE: Why Fixed-Fee Consulting Engagements Are Replacing Time-and-Materials in Manufacturing
As manufacturers grow wary of open-ended consulting spend, a growing share of operations engagements are structured as fixed-fee, milestone-based contracts. We spoke with three boutique advisory firms about how they scope and price this way without eating the risk of scope creep — a theme worth watching if your own engagements are trending the same direction.

DATA: Q2 industrial production ticked up 1.4% quarter over quarter, driven largely by durable goods. Capacity utilization remains below the 15-year average, suggesting continued appetite for efficiency-focused consulting engagements over pure capacity expansion.

PEOPLE MOVES: Ridgefield Mfg names a new VP of Operations; three other executive moves across the Midwest manufacturing corridor.

TOOLS: A roundup of five ERP add-ons gaining traction with mid-market manufacturers this quarter, including two aimed specifically at improving forecast accuracy for make-to-order shops. Several readers wrote in after last month's issue asking for more detail on implementation timelines, so this roundup includes real customer-reported rollout windows rather than vendor marketing estimates — most ran 4 to 7 months longer than initially quoted, a pattern worth flagging to any client currently evaluating a system change.

DEEP DIVE: THE CONSULTANT'S ROLE IN CAPEX DECISIONS
A growing number of manufacturers are bringing outside advisors into capital equipment decisions earlier than in past cycles, not just for post-purchase process design. We interviewed five plant-level finance leaders who described a shift from "call the consultant once the machine is installed" to "get a second opinion before the PO is cut." For advisory firms, this means capex evaluation frameworks and vendor-neutral ROI modeling are becoming a more explicit part of the sales conversation, not an afterthought bundled into a broader engagement.

LABOR MARKET WATCH: Wage growth for skilled manufacturing roles held at 5.8% year over year in the Midwest, slightly ahead of the national average. Several members report that overtime costs, not base wage inflation, are now the bigger line-item pressure, driven by continued difficulty filling second and third shifts.

subject: Re: Meridian diagnostic data — throughput analysis
snippet: Evelyn, About 80% through the modeling — attached is the working draft with what I've confirmed so far, and I want to walk through the headline finding because it's more interestin
body_text:
Evelyn,

About 80% through the modeling — attached is the working draft with what I've confirmed so far, and I want to walk through the headline finding because it's more interesting than I expected going in.

I pulled six weeks of MES data across all three of Meridian's production lines and normalized for shift patterns and the two planned maintenance windows in that period. Line A (core casting) is running at 94 seconds average cycle time against a theoretical target of 78 seconds, giving it 71% utilization, with Station 4 — the cooling stage — as the clear local bottleneck. Line B (finishing) is actually in decent shape at 84% utilization, 61 seconds against a 55-second target, constrained mildly at Station 2 (deburr) but nothing dramatic.

The real story is Line C, the satellite line at the Rockford facility. It's running at only 58% utilization, 118 seconds against a 90-second target, and the constraint is Station 1, mold prep, which is running almost entirely manually while the equivalent stations on Lines A and B have partial automation. Because Line C feeds into downstream shared packaging capacity, the model suggests this is actually the binding constraint on total plant throughput, not Line A, which is what everyone on the plant floor assumed going in. Closing even half the gap at Station 1 — without any capital investment, just changeover and staffing adjustments — could add an estimated 12-15% to overall plant output. That's a much more useful finding for Bob's board update than "we found some inefficiencies," and it's the kind of thing that justifies the fixed fee on its own.

Remaining work: I still need to validate the Line C numbers against a second data pull since the sample size there is thinner (fewer shifts logged, Rockford runs two shifts not three), and I want to sanity-check the maintenance-window exclusions with their plant engineer before I call it final. Should have a validated final version to you by Monday.

One more thing worth flagging now rather than burying it in the final report: if the Line C finding holds up under the second data pull, it changes the framing of the whole recommendations section. The original brief assumed we'd be recommending investment across all three lines roughly proportionally. If Line C really is the binding constraint, the honest recommendation is probably to concentrate almost all of the near-term operational changes there and treat Lines A and B as secondary, which is a more concentrated, less balanced-sounding story than what I think Bob's team may be expecting walking in. Wanted you to have that heads-up before Monday so it's not a surprise in the readout, and so you can decide how you want to frame it for the board update.

Anil

subject: Re: Partner comp — thinking ahead to next year
snippet: Gordon, Spent some time with the numbers before Friday so we're not starting from a blank page. Here's my thinking. The 60/40 split made sense when it was set: you'd brought in the
body_text:
Gordon,

Spent some time with the numbers before Friday so we're not starting from a blank page. Here's my thinking.

The 60/40 split made sense when it was set: you'd brought in the original Meridian and Ridgefield relationships and I was doing more of the delivery work. That's shifted. Looking at this year through July: I originated Stratus, the Halberd renewal, and the expanded Meridian phase 2 scope — roughly $340K of the $480K we've booked or have in late-stage pipeline. You originated the Meridian phase 1 relationship years back (which is still generating revenue and deserves credit) and have been carrying more of the firm-admin load this year — the insurance renewal, the lease renegotiation, onboarding the new hire process with Sheila. That's real value that a pure origination split doesn't capture.

So rather than just moving the split number, I want to propose a different structure entirely: a formula-based comp model with three components. First, a base draw that's equal between us, reflecting that we're both full-time and both carry real responsibility regardless of who's closing what. Second, an origination credit pool — a percentage of revenue attributed to whoever brought in the client relationship, which would have tilted toward me this year but tilted toward you in year one when you brought in Meridian and Ridgefield. Third, a firm-building credit — things like recruiting, ops, and the admin load that don't show up in origination numbers but keep the place running. That third bucket is honestly where I think the current structure undervalues what you've been doing this year.

I'd want to model this against both 2024 and 2025 actuals before either of us commits to anything — want to make sure it doesn't produce a wild swing in either direction based on one good or bad year. If the historical numbers hold up, I think this gets us to something closer to 55/45 in my favor this particular year, but with the structure set up so it can swing the other way in a year where you're the one bringing in the big relationship. That feels fairer than a fixed split either of us has to argue about again in three years.

Open to pushback on any of this — wanted to get a real proposal in front of you rather than just vague 'let's talk about it' energy.

Evelyn

Evelyn Thorne
President, Thorne & Cadwell Advisory
312-555-0148

body_text:
Evelyn,

Went through the Phase 2 SOW with our ops team and finance this week. Overall we're comfortable moving forward — the scope matches what we discussed on the call two weeks ago and the $185K number is in line with what we budgeted for the diagnostic phase. A few items I redlined in the attached before this goes to procurement for countersignature:

1. Payment terms — I need NET-30 instead of NET-15. Our AP cycle runs on a monthly batch and NET-15 means we'd be cutting a check outside the normal run, which our controller doesn't love. NET-30 gets us into the regular cycle.

2. Data room access — the draft has data access starting "after kickoff." I'd rather your team (sounds like that's mostly Dr. Bose doing the throughput modeling?) have read access to our MES exports starting the same week as kickoff so we don't lose the first week waiting on IT to provision accounts. Our IT director can set this up in advance if you flag the usernames now.

3. One clarifying question on the interim findings memo — is that a working draft for our internal use only, or will it also go to our board? We had a board update scheduled for week 4 and it would help to know if that memo is presentable as-is or needs a different format.

4. Small thing — Section 6 still references "Phase 1 findings" using the old project code MC-2025-11. Should be MC-2026-04 to match the engagement letter.

5. One more from our CFO — she'd like the final report delivered in a format that can be dropped directly into our board deck without a lot of reformatting, meaning charts as editable PowerPoint objects rather than embedded images, since the last time we tried to pull a chart out of a PDF appendix it took our analyst half a day to recreate it. Not a big lift I'd guess, but wanted to flag it now rather than have it come up as a surprise at delivery.

None of these are dealbreakers on our end. If you can turn a clean version with these changes I can get this to our procurement lead by end of week and we should be able to countersign before the 15th. Also — appreciate you and Gordon walking our ops committee through the approach last month, it made this internal approval a lot smoother than Phase 1 was.

Talk soon,
Bob

Bob Vandergriff

From: Lucia Ferraro <l.ferraro@halberdpackaging.com>
Date: Thu, Jul 30, 2026 at 4:47 PM
Subject: Halberd — need updated inventory turns numbers
To: Kyle Brenner <kyle.brenner@thornecadwell.com>
Cc: Ana Restrepo <ana.restrepo@thornecadwell.com>

Kyle,

I need you to pull together the updated inventory turns analysis before our ops review Thursday morning, and I mean the real numbers, not the placeholder deck from the kickoff. Our warehouse team flagged yesterday that finished-goods turns on the injection-molded line have been sliding for six straight weeks and nobody upstairs believes it's just seasonal. I told the plant manager you'd have something concrete by end of day Wednesday so he can walk into the review with an actual explanation instead of a shrug.

Specifically I need:
- Turns by SKU family for the top 40 SKUs by volume, June and July, compared to the Q1 baseline you built
- A breakdown of the three SKUs we flagged in the May workshop (the 4-inch coupling assemblies, the gasket kits, and the bracket sub-assembly) since those are the ones burning the most floor space
- Your read on whether the slowdown tracks with the new customer allocation rules we rolled out in June, because two of our regional sales leads are convinced it does and I want either confirmation or a clean rebuttal

For context, our finished-goods carrying cost on that line is running about $38,000 a month higher than the Q1 baseline, and if turns don't recover before the Q3 close I'm going to have a hard time explaining that to Marcus (our CFO), let alone the board.

I know you've also got the Meridian ramp-up eating your week, and I don't love piling this on top, but the board is going to ask about working capital and I need someone who actually understands the WMS export in the room with real answers, not me improvising off a stale spreadsheet. If Thursday morning genuinely isn't realistic given everything else on your plate, tell me today so I can push the review or find another way to cover it — but please don't let me find out Wednesday night that it's not going to happen.

Ana, looping you in mainly so you know why Kyle might be heads-down the next two days. Appreciate you both.

Lucia

Lucia Ferraro
COO, Halberd Packaging

subject: Utilization, and why I keep bugging you about timesheets
snippet: Team, Quick note on something that's been nagging at me, and I'd rather say it plainly than keep dropping hints in Monday standups. July utilization across the firm was 68%. Target
body_text:
Team,

Quick note on something that's been nagging at me, and I'd rather say it plainly than keep dropping hints in Monday standups.

July utilization across the firm was 68%. Target is 78-80% for a firm our size to actually make the economics work — below that and we're either underpricing engagements or overstaffing them, and right now it's a bit of both. Ana and Kyle are both over 85%, which is genuinely too high and part of why I'm pulling myself back into a supervisory role on Meridian instead of running it day-to-day. Fiona, you're closer to 55%, partly timing, partly that Ridgefield and Halberd haven't kept you as busy as I'd like — that changes fast once Stratus kicks off, so don't read this as a complaint about you specifically.

The bigger issue is timesheet accuracy. I know it's the most annoying part of the job, and I know I am, personally, the worst offender — Sheila can confirm I'm usually three days late entering my own hours, which is a bad example to set while also asking everyone else to be diligent about it. I'm going to fix that on my end starting this week, timesheets entered same-day, no exceptions, and I'd ask the same of everyone else.

Here's why it actually matters beyond bookkeeping: every fixed-fee engagement we scope depends on knowing what similar work actually costs us in hours, not what we guessed it would cost. Halberd is a good example — we scoped it at 120 hours based on a rough gut-check, and it's at 165 and climbing, which means either our historical data was thin or nobody trusted it. Accurate time data going forward means better proposals, which means better margins, which is directly connected to whether we can afford the fifth-consultant hire I've been talking about for two quarters and am finally moving on this month.

I'm not trying to turn this into a big-firm bureaucracy exercise. I just want us pricing our time as if it's worth what it's worth, which means actually knowing what things cost. Ten people is small enough that we can still fix this with a plain email instead of buying software for it, so let's not overbuild the solution either.

Sheila — can you send a utilization breakdown by person, monthly, starting with July? I want it as a standing agenda item at Monday standup going forward, not a once-a-quarter surprise when Gordon and I are trying to close the books.

One more thing while I have everyone's attention: if you're consistently over 85%, tell me. I'd rather hear "I'm underwater" in a Tuesday message than find out in an exit interview. We're hiring a fifth consultant partly because of this exact conversation, and I want the hire to actually land before anyone burns out waiting for it.

Thanks for reading this far. Back to it.

Evelyn

subject: Where we stand heading into Q4 — capacity and the fifth hire
snippet: Gordon, Ana — Wanted to get ahead of Q4 planning with where things actually stand, since I don't think we've stepped back and looked at the whole board together in a few weeks. Pip
body_text:
Gordon, Ana —

Wanted to get ahead of Q4 planning with where things actually stand, since I don't think we've stepped back and looked at the whole board together in a few weeks.

Pipeline: Stratus is close — Owen's board approved roughly $90K for the supply chain diagnostic and we're finalizing scope now (Terre Haute handled as a remote review rather than a full on-site to make the number work). That should sign by mid-August and start the week after. Meridian phase 2 is underway, Ana leading on-site with Kyle supporting remotely alongside Anil — that's a six-week engagement running through late September, and if it goes well I think there's a real phase 3 conversation about extending into their Toledo facility. Halberd is wrapping in the next three weeks; we're over budgeted hours there (Kyle's already flagged it to me separately) but the relationship is solid and I expect a renewal conversation once the QBR cycle settles. Ridgefield is basically closed out — final deck goes out later this month — but I made a complimentary follow-up offer to Marta back in June that I've had to walk back given everything else on our plate, which stings a little but was the right call.

Put together, that's three active engagements plus a fourth about to start, against five billable people including me. Utilization has been fine through the summer but I don't think it holds through Q4 if Stratus and any Meridian extension both land — we'd be stretched thin exactly when we need to be sharpest with two of our biggest relationships.

I want to open a req for a fifth consultant. Target profile: 3-5 years in operations or supply chain consulting, comfortable running client-facing workstreams with light oversight, ideally someone who's touched manufacturing or industrial clients specifically rather than generalist strategy work — we don't have bandwidth to train someone up on plant-floor fluency from scratch. Budget-wise I think we can support a $95-115K base plus our standard bonus structure without straining anything, especially once Stratus signs.

I'd like to have someone identified by end of September and starting by November at the latest, so they're ramped before the January proposal season starts back up. I'll reach out to our usual network first and put a LinkedIn post up if that doesn't turn up anyone in the next couple weeks. Let me know if either of you has someone in mind before I start casting a wider net — always rather hire off a warm reference than a cold applicant pool.

Happy to talk through any of this at Monday's partner meeting if useful.

Evelyn
